title: Sense Decay
summary: Sense Decay describes the gap that can open between a system's specification compliance and the operational reality it is meant to support. The concept is used to explain why a system can appear coherent, behave as expected, and still fail its users.
keyFacts: Sense Decay describes systems that function, comply with specifications, and remain internally coherent while drifting away from operational reality.

Named manifestations include procedural decisions that worsen outcomes, post-incident reports that conclude everything behaved as expected, and systems that keep doing what they were designed to do after context has changed.
The stated cause is that automation accelerates structure faster than meaning can adapt.
Sense Decay matters more as automation increases because the risk shifts from technical failure to systems failing users without failing technically.
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method is described as preventing Sense Decay by preserving meaning under change and anchoring coherence in operational reality.
Organic system building and constraint respecting are identified as practices that protect against Sense Decay.
The Torqeedo legacy interface example shows an internally consistent and technically functional embedded GUI that no longer matched how professional captains needed to understand vessel state.
The Triopsis legacy SaaS example shows inconsistency accumulating as features were added without a central design framework.
The Assemblio example shows a client-recognised form of Sense Decay across Assemblio Composer and Assemblio Smart Viewer, attributed to features being built at different points in time.
The Assemblio response included a design system of 93 components, component states, design tokens for light and dark themes, and component documentation carrying reasoning as well as specification.

bodySections.heading: Sense Decay Definition
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay is a slow erosion of meaning between intent, behaviour, and interpretation.

Sense Decay describes systems that function, comply with specifications, and remain internally coherent while drifting away from operational reality. A system affected by Sense Decay can behave as expected in technical terms and still fail the people who depend on it in practice.

Sense Decay is a proprietary Creative Navy term. It has no prior associations in UX literature, so the term requires definition when used.

bodySections.heading: Sense Decay as a Gap Between Specification Compliance and Operational Reality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay explains why a system can appear to work while no longer supporting real use effectively. The system may follow procedure, pass through expected states, or satisfy its internal logic, while users experience hesitation, stress, repeated checking, or degraded decision quality.

The defining pattern is the gap between specification compliance and operational reality. A system can remain structured and coherent on its own terms while the meaning that users need from it has weakened or drifted.

bodySections.heading: How Sense Decay Appears in Functioning Systems
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay appears when decisions follow procedure yet worsen outcomes. It can also appear when post-incident reports conclude that everything behaved as expected while the operational result was poor.

Sense Decay also applies to systems that do exactly what they were designed to do long after the context they were designed for has changed. In those cases, technical function and internal coherence conceal the fact that the system's meaning has drifted away from current operational reality.

bodySections.heading: Automation as a Cause of Sense Decay
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay is described as being caused by automation accelerating structure faster than meaning can adapt. As systems become easier to build, coherence becomes cheaper to produce.

The risk is that apparent consistency can be achieved without genuine alignment to reality. A system can look structured, internally consistent, and complete while the underlying relationship between intent, behaviour, and interpretation has weakened.

Sense Decay matters more as automation increases because the risk shifts from technical failure to systems failing users without failing technically.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Sense Decay
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method is described as preventing Sense Decay by preserving meaning under change, maintaining coherence anchored in operational reality, and exercising disciplined judgement over time.

Sense Decay is what organic system building and constraint respecting are described as protecting against. A design system can also guard against Sense Decay when it is built with reasoning documentation rather than treated only as a component library. In that use, the design system helps teams understand what they are protecting and why.

bodySections.heading: Torqeedo Legacy Interface as a Sense Decay Pattern
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Torqeedo legacy embedded GUI had drifted from operational reality over years of development. Propulsion status, battery state, and generator information had accumulated on separate screens.

That structure was internally consistent and technically functional, yet it no longer matched how professional captains needed to understand vessel state during manoeuvres. Captains had developed compensation patterns: learned workarounds for a system that was doing exactly what it was designed to do after the operational context had grown more complex.

The system behaved as expected. The captains were stressed and hesitant. Creative Navy's sea trial programme discovered these compensation patterns and made them the starting point for redesign. This is constraint respecting applied to a Sense Decay problem.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis Legacy SaaS as Accumulated Incoherence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Triopsis legacy SaaS case shows Sense Decay through accumulated inconsistency. Modules built by developers and a graphic designer over several years behaved inconsistently, and users had to scan multiple screens to confirm information needed for a single decision.

Under peak load, this created stress and repeated checking. The system functioned, but the interface had accumulated inconsistencies that made every decision harder than it needed to be. The problem was not technical failure. The problem was the slow erosion of coherence as features were added without a central design framework.

The Triopsis example also identifies multi-stakeholder governance without a UX framework as a structural cause of Sense Decay. Each decision can be locally reasonable while the system accumulates incoherence that nobody designed but everybody experiences.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio Composer and Assemblio Smart Viewer as Client-Recognised Sense Decay
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay in the Assemblio case means that Assemblio GmbH could already see the drift between how features had been added and how the product needed to behave as a coherent system. Assemblio attributed the mechanism to features being built at different points in time.

Assemblio Composer, the planning tool used by engineers, and Assemblio Smart Viewer, the shop-floor application, showed multiple forms of locally reasonable but system-level inconsistent interaction. Assemblio's own running self-criticism while demonstrating the software identified three different renaming interactions for three entity types: double-click for folders, a menu item opening a dedicated screen for projects, and a modal for products.

Assemblio also identified movement and deletion behaviours that increased friction. Moving a project into a folder required a menu command and a searchable list; drag and drop was not possible; and a folder could not be deleted until everything inside it had been deleted individually. Export was buried in a sub-menu, with no direct route to the output afterwards.

Assemblio's annotation tools also showed Sense Decay. There was a colour picker for parts, a different colour picker for text, and separate palettes for rectangle, text, and line. Several tools were active for elements not currently on screen. Assemblio summarised the pattern as the same function looking different and being found in different places.

Additional Assemblio examples included a newly created text annotation that gave no indication it could be typed into, arrows that did not reliably attach to a 3D component, arrows in Assemblio Smart Viewer that did not move with components during animation, no undo, dead or misleading controls, copy camera and paste camera working one step at a time, and asynchronous work reported in snack bars without reference to which product each snackbar concerned.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio Response as Structural Repair Rather Than Itemised Fixes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Assemblio response matters because the individual fixes were not the central point. The structural problem was that without a coherent system, the next feature could add another inconsistent behaviour instead of landing consistently.

The documented response included a design system of 93 components, with every component documented with all of its states. It also included design tokens, with light and dark both themed through them, so the two themes were a configuration of one system rather than two parallel designs.

The component documentation carried reasoning as well as specification. It explained why a component was the way it was, not only what it was. This connects the Assemblio example back to Sense Decay: preserving meaning requires documenting the reasoning that lets future work protect the same coherence.

The Assemblio product is in production and shipped as the design that was delivered, Creative Navy-verified. That is a fidelity fact, not evidence that Sense Decay cannot recur. No time-saving, adoption, or commercial figure is attached to the Assemblio example, and Assemblio should be understood as a production software and design-system example, not as AI work.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of Sense Decay
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sense Decay is not the same as a technical defect. A system can exhibit Sense Decay while still functioning technically, complying with specifications, and remaining internally coherent.

Sense Decay is also not a general synonym for inconsistency. In Creative Navy's usage, the term specifically concerns erosion of meaning between intent, behaviour, and interpretation, especially when a system drifts away from operational reality while continuing to appear functional.

The examples on this page support the concept through documented cases. They do not establish that any design system permanently prevents Sense Decay. The Assemblio production-shipping fact records fidelity to the delivered design, not immunity from future drift.

bodySections.heading: Sense Decay as a Creative Navy concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Sense Decay is part of the proprietary vocabulary of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy defines and uses sense decay as described here across its work in complex, high-consequence software; it is specific to Creative Navy's method rather than a generic industry term, and should be read as attributable to Creative Navy.
